note: Mechanism-based support protocols. Researched and then adversarially verified against primary sources; evidenceStrength is per protocol and mechanistic inference is labelled as such.

protocols.bodyEffect: Your dreams get louder and stranger. The drug pushes REM sleep out of its usual slots, so it comes back in longer, more vivid bursts.
protocols.mechanism: Serotonin suppresses REM sleep and delays its onset, so REM gets compressed and then returns in denser, more emotionally charged blocks.
doThis: Expect it, and do not read the dreams as meaning anything. Vivid or unpleasant dreams in the first weeks are a pharmacology artefact, not your subconscious telling you something.
Take the dose at the same time every day. Erratic timing lets the level dip and makes the REM rebound sharper.
If a dream wakes you, get out of bed, keep the light low, do something dull for 15 minutes, then go back. Do not lie there replaying it.
If dreams are still disturbing past week 6, say so. Moving the dose earlier in the day sometimes helps.
avoidThis: Alcohol as a way to blunt the dreams. It suppresses REM early in the night and makes the rebound worse in the second half, which is the half already under pressure.
protocols.timeline: Strongest in the first 2-3 weeks, and again after any dose increase. Usually fades by week 4-6 for most people.
protocols.source: Polysomnography consistently shows REM suppression and increased REM latency with SSRIs, SNRIs and TCAs (Wilson & Argyropoulos, Drugs 2005). The step from measured REM suppression to subjectively intense dreams is mechanistic inference, not a measured endpoint. No per-drug percentage figures are given because the polysomnography literature is too heterogeneous to support them.

protocols.bodyEffect: These raise noradrenaline or dopamine as well as serotonin. That is a stimulant-like push: useful at 9am, ruinous at 11pm.
protocols.mechanism: Noradrenergic and dopaminergic tone raises cortical arousal, which is the exact signal the brain uses to stay awake, so an evening dose is competing directly with sleep onset.
doThis: Take it in the morning, within about an hour of waking. Anchor it to breakfast so you do not have to remember it separately.
On a twice-daily form, get the second dose in by early afternoon.
Use the push rather than fighting it: put the walk, the shower, the hardest task of the day in the hours after the dose.
If it is keeping you awake past week 3, that is a dose-timing or dose-size conversation, not something to endure.
avoidThis: Moving the dose to bedtime to sleep through the nausea. You trade nausea for insomnia and usually lose.
Doubling up after a missed dose. Take the next one at the normal time.
protocols.timeline: Activation and early insomnia peak in weeks 1-2 and usually settle by week 4 for most people.
protocols.source: Downgraded from 'label'. What the labels actually support: insomnia and nervousness are listed among common adverse effects for fluoxetine, venlafaxine and sertraline, and the bupropion SR label specifies dose separation and advises against bedtime dosing. The labels do not instruct morning dosing for SSRIs or SNRIs, and no trial has tested morning versus evening dosing for these drugs. The 'use the activation window' advice is practical inference.

protocols.bodyEffect: Bupropion is the odd one out. It does not flatten REM sleep the way serotonin drugs do. If anything it does the reverse.
protocols.mechanism: It blocks noradrenaline and dopamine reuptake rather than serotonin, so the serotonergic brake on REM is never applied. Sleep studies show it lengthens REM latency and increases REM density rather than suppressing REM.
doThis: Morning dosing. On the twice-daily SR form leave at least 8 hours between doses and get the second one in before mid-afternoon.
If insomnia is the main complaint, ask whether the once-daily XL form taken in the morning would suit you better.
Watch caffeine hard in the first fortnight. Bupropion and caffeine stack on the same arousal axis and this is where jitteriness comes from.
If you get vivid dreams on bupropion, it is not a sign something is wrong. Bupropion increases REM measures rather than suppressing them, and dream intensity is reported on it.
protocols.timeline: Insomnia is most common in the first 1-2 weeks and often improves from there.
protocols.source: CORRECTED. Ott et al., Psychopharmacology 2002;165:29-36 found bupropion-SR lengthened REM latency and increased REM activity and density, i.e. bupropion is a REM enhancer, not REM-neutral (see also Nofzinger et al. 1995, 'REM sleep enhancement by bupropion'). The previous version's advice that vivid dreams on bupropion mean 'something else is going on' was the opposite of what the evidence supports and has been removed. The claim that bupropion does not cause limb movements is from the PLMS meta-analysis below, whose authors explicitly say the absent effect for non-SSRI drugs needs confirmation.

protocols.bodyEffect: The sedation is a strong antihistamine effect, closer to an old allergy tablet than a sleeping pill. It is heavy and it is front-loaded.
protocols.mechanism: Mirtazapine strongly blocks histamine H1 receptors, and histamine is the brain's main wakefulness signal, so the sedation is deepest in the hours right after the dose.
doThis: Take it 1-2 hours before you actually intend to be asleep, not as you get into bed. You want the peak landing while you are already lying down.
Give yourself a 9-10 hour window in bed for the first fortnight. The morning hangover mostly comes from being woken mid-sedation.
If you are flattened all morning, try moving the dose earlier in the evening before asking to change the dose.
Do not drive in the morning until you have tested how clear you actually are, particularly in week 1.
avoidThis: Alcohol. The sedation is additive and genuinely dangerous, not just unpleasant.
Stacking an over-the-counter sedating antihistamine on top. You are hitting the same receptor twice.
protocols.timeline: Heaviest in weeks 1-2, then eases substantially for most people by week 3-4.
protocols.source: Somnolence is the most frequently reported adverse effect in the mirtazapine label, which also warns about impaired judgement and motor skills and about additive impairment with alcohol. H1 antagonism is the accepted mechanism. The widely repeated claim that lower doses (7.5-15mg) are MORE sedating than higher doses is receptor-pharmacology reasoning plus clinical convention, not trial evidence. It must never be surfaced as a standalone tip and must never be used to argue for a dose increase.

protocols.bodyEffect: At low doses trazodone sedates through histamine and alpha-1 blockade, and unlike most antidepressants it adds deep slow-wave sleep rather than reshaping REM.
protocols.mechanism: Trazodone blocks 5-HT2A receptors alongside H1 and alpha-1 receptors; at 25-100mg the sedating receptor blockade dominates and serotonin reuptake inhibition is minimal, which is why it sedates without the REM suppression pattern of SSRIs.
doThis: Take it 30-60 minutes before bed. Expect deeper, heavier sleep rather than being knocked out.
Stand up slowly if you get up in the night. The alpha-1 blockade drops your blood pressure and the dizziness at 3am is real, not imagined.
Hold realistic expectations. In the trial the sleep-medicine guideline relied on, 50mg shortened time to fall asleep by about 10 minutes and added about 22 minutes of total sleep.
Men: an erection lasting over 4 hours is a medical emergency, not something to sleep off. It is rare, but go to the emergency department the same night.
avoidThis: Treating it as a powerful sleeping pill. The measured effect is modest and the specialist guideline is mildly against using it for insomnia, which does not mean your prescriber is wrong, but you should know the evidence you are working with.
protocols.timeline: Works from the first night. Unlike the antidepressant effect there is no build-up period to wait through.
protocols.source: AASM 2017 Clinical Practice Guideline (J Clin Sleep Med 13:307): weak recommendation AGAINST trazodone for sleep-onset or sleep-maintenance insomnia, based on a 50mg trial showing sleep latency reduced 10.2 min, total sleep time +21.8 min, WASO reduced 7.7 min, all below clinical significance thresholds. Verified. Slow-wave sleep increase: polysomnographic meta-analysis in insomnia disorder, 2022. CORRECTED: the previous claim that low-dose trazodone avoids 'the REM suppression seen at full antidepressant doses' implied a dose-dependent REM effect that I could not source, and has been removed.

protocols.bodyEffect: Caffeine and an activating antidepressant press the same anxiety and insomnia buttons. In the early weeks you may be more sensitive than you used to be.
protocols.mechanism: Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors, stripping away the sleep pressure that has been building all day, and raises arousal on the same axis the drug is already pushing.
doThis: Last caffeine by about 2pm. The half-life is roughly 5 hours, so a 4pm coffee still has around a third of its dose in you at midnight.
Halve your usual intake for the first 3-4 weeks, then rebuild slowly. Do not quit outright or you add a withdrawal headache to an already bad fortnight.
If your normal coffee now makes you jittery, shaky or racing, that is most likely this interaction rather than a new heart problem, but mention it at your next appointment.
protocols.timeline: Heightened caffeine sensitivity, where it happens, tracks the activation phase, usually weeks 1-4.
protocols.source: Caffeine's ~5 hour half-life (range 3-7h, wider in pregnancy and with oral contraceptives) and adenosine antagonism are established pharmacology. CORRECTED: the previous version said a 4pm coffee leaves 'around a quarter' at midnight; at a 5h half-life, 8 hours leaves about a third. DELETED: the 'delay your first coffee 90 minutes' tip, which is popular internet advice with no good supporting evidence and reads as wellness filler. The core claim, that antidepressant starters are more caffeine-sensitive, remains untested inference from shared arousal pathways.

protocols.bodyEffect: On fluvoxamine, caffeine stops leaving your body. One cup can behave like several and stay in your system all day and all night.
protocols.mechanism: Fluvoxamine is a potent inhibitor of CYP1A2, the liver enzyme that clears caffeine, so caffeine accumulates instead of wearing off.
doThis: Cut caffeine hard. One small morning cup, or none. This is the single biggest sleep lever available to you on this drug, bigger than any bedtime routine.
Count the hidden sources: strong tea, green tea, cola, energy drinks, dark chocolate, some combination painkillers and cold remedies.
If you feel wired, sweaty, tremulous or your heart is pounding, caffeine accumulation is the most likely explanation, and cutting caffeine is the first thing to try.
Tell any new prescriber you are on fluvoxamine. The same enzyme handles several other drugs, so this is not only about coffee.
avoidThis: Energy drinks, entirely.
Treating the tiredness with more coffee. On fluvoxamine you accumulate rather than get a lift, and the payment comes at 2am.

Assuming it must be caffeine if you also have muscle twitching or jerks, fever, agitation or diarrhoea alongside the sweating and racing heart. That combination needs urgent medical assessment, not a smaller coffee.
protocols.timeline: Present as soon as fluvoxamine reaches steady state, within about a week of starting, and lasts the entire time you take it. This one does not adapt away.
protocols.source: Jeppesen et al., Pharmacogenetics 1996 (n=8 crossover): during fluvoxamine, median caffeine clearance fell from 107 to 21 mL/min and half-life rose from 5 to 31 hours. VERIFIED against the primary abstract. Replicated by Culm-Merdek et al., Br J Clin Pharmacol 2005. The fluvoxamine label carries CYP1A2 interaction warnings (contraindications and warnings for CYP1A2 substrates including tizanidine, theophylline and clozapine); I softened the previous wording, which implied a caffeine-specific label warning. SAFETY ADDITION: the wired/sweaty/racing symptom list overlaps with serotonin syndrome, so the previous instruction to blame caffeine first has been given a red-flag caveat.

protocols.bodyEffect: Antidepressants change when you feel sleepy but do not reset your body clock. Light is what moves the clock, and it works within days.
protocols.mechanism: Morning light hits melanopsin cells in the retina that set the master clock in the suprachiasmatic nucleus, advancing that evening's melatonin release. That is a separate lever from the drug, so the two stack.
doThis: Get outside within 30-60 minutes of waking, for 10-20 minutes, no sunglasses. An overcast morning outdoors is still many times brighter than a well-lit room.
If you cannot get out, eat breakfast next to the brightest window in the house, or use a 10,000 lux light box for 30 minutes.
Dim the house from about two hours before bed. It is light intensity and timing that matter, not screens specifically.
Hold your wake time fixed, weekends included. A fixed wake time anchors the clock more strongly than a fixed bedtime.
protocols.timeline: Circadian shifts need 3-7 days of consistency before they show. Any mood benefit takes longer, on the order of 2-4 weeks.
protocols.source: Bright light therapy meta-analyses in non-seasonal depression show benefit at around 10,000 lux for 30-60 minutes daily (Golden et al., Am J Psychiatry 2005 and later reviews). Using light specifically to counteract antidepressant-related sleep disruption has not been trialled as an indication and is a mechanistic extension. If someone has bipolar disorder, light scheduling should be discussed with their prescriber, since bright light can destabilise mood.

protocols.bodyEffect: Exercise raises sleep pressure and deepens deep sleep. It is one of the few things that helps both the daytime flatness and the night.
protocols.mechanism: Physical activity increases slow-wave (deep) sleep and lengthens REM latency, partly offsetting the sleep-architecture changes the drug is causing.
doThis: Aim for moderate activity most days. Morning or early afternoon pairs well with activating drugs; late afternoon works well if you are on something sedating.
You do not need to avoid evening exercise. The pooled evidence says it does not harm sleep and slightly improves it. The exception is vigorous exercise finishing less than an hour before bed.
On a sedating drug, use a short walk to break the afternoon dip instead of napping. It gets you through without spending tonight's sleep pressure.
Start absurdly small if you are depressed. Ten minutes of walking counts and beats an unmet intention to do forty-five.
protocols.timeline: Sleep-architecture effects show within days to a couple of weeks of consistent activity.
protocols.source: Stutz et al., Sports Medicine 2019, 23 studies: evening exercise increased REM latency by 7.7 min and slow-wave sleep by 1.3 percentage points, and reduced stage 1 sleep; impairment of sleep onset, total sleep time and efficiency appeared only with vigorous exercise ending 1 hour or less before bed. VERIFIED. Note the effect sizes are small, and all participants were healthy, so applying this to people on antidepressants is reasonable extension rather than direct evidence.

protocols.bodyEffect: The 3pm wall is real. Fragmented night sleep, leftover sedation and your natural circadian dip all arrive at the same hour.
protocols.mechanism: The body has a genuine circadian trough in early-to-mid afternoon; antidepressant sleep fragmentation and residual sedation turn a normal dip into a wall.
doThis: Treat it as a scheduling problem, not a willpower problem. Put low-cognitive work in the 2-4pm window and defend the morning for anything hard.
Get 10-20 minutes of outdoor daylight at the dip. It is the second most useful light exposure of the day and it does not cost you tonight's sleep the way coffee does.
Move for 5-10 minutes. A brisk walk raises arousal without borrowing against your sleep.
Eat a lunch that includes protein rather than being carbohydrate alone.
eatThis: Protein at lunch, around 25-30g: eggs, fish, chicken, beans, Greek yoghurt. Large carbohydrate-heavy meals deepen post-lunch sleepiness more than mixed meals do
protocols.timeline: Worst in weeks 1-3, usually much better by week 4-6 once night sleep consolidates.
protocols.source: The post-lunch circadian dip is established sleep physiology. The meal-composition effect on post-prandial sleepiness is real but small and inconsistent in the literature, and none of it was measured in people starting antidepressants. DELETED: the 'drink water, mild dehydration reads as fatigue' item. It was generic wellness filler, and telling people on SSRIs and SNRIs to drink more water is the wrong default given hyponatraemia risk (see ssri-hyponatraemia-fluid-safety).

protocols.bodyEffect: These drugs can make your body hold on to water, which dilutes your blood sodium. It feels like tiredness, headache, unsteadiness and fuzzy thinking, which is exactly what you would otherwise blame on the depression.
protocols.mechanism: Serotonergic antidepressants can trigger inappropriate release of antidiuretic hormone (SIADH), so the kidneys reabsorb water the body does not need and sodium concentration falls.
doThis: Drink to thirst. Do not force large volumes of plain water to 'flush out' side effects or fix fatigue. On these drugs that advice can push sodium down rather than help.

Know the red flags: worsening headache, confusion, unsteadiness on your feet, new nausea, or muscle cramps and weakness in the first weeks. Get a same-week blood test, and same-day assessment if you are confused or unsteady.
If you are over 65, low body weight, or taking a diuretic, ask whether a sodium check before starting and again at around two weeks is worth doing. That combination is where most cases occur.
If you are exercising hard or in hot weather, replace salt as well as fluid rather than water alone.
avoidThis: Stopping the drug on your own if you suspect this. It needs a blood test and a prescriber decision, and abrupt stopping adds discontinuation symptoms on top.
protocols.timeline: Usually within the first few weeks of starting or of a dose increase. Risk falls after that but does not disappear.
protocols.source: ADDED by this review, because the set previously contained generic 'drink water' advice with no counterweight. Hyponatraemia and SIADH appear in the Warnings and Precautions section of SSRI and SNRI labels, which name elderly patients and those on diuretics or volume-depleted as higher risk and list headache, difficulty concentrating, memory impairment, confusion, weakness and unsteadiness as symptoms. Onset within weeks of initiation is consistent with the case and cohort literature. Frequency figures are not given here because published incidence estimates vary too widely by population and sodium threshold to quote a single number.

protocols.bodyEffect: Early insomnia on an antidepressant is arousal, not a shortage of tiredness. Lying there trying harder teaches your brain that bed means awake.
protocols.mechanism: Raised noradrenergic tone keeps cortical arousal high even when sleep pressure is genuinely there, and staying in bed awake conditions the brain to associate the bed with wakefulness.
doThis: If you have been awake 20-25 minutes, get up. Different room, dim light, something dull and paper-based. Go back only when sleepy. Repeat as many times as the night requires.
Keep your wake time fixed even after a terrible night. Sleeping in to compensate is what turns two bad nights into three bad weeks.
Turn the clock away from you. Watching the time converts tiredness into anxiety within minutes.
Give it 10-14 days before you conclude the drug does not suit you. Most early insomnia genuinely resolves, and day four is the worst possible moment to judge.
avoidThis: Alcohol. It shortens sleep onset then fragments the second half of the night, which is already the vulnerable half on these drugs.
Nightly over-the-counter sedating antihistamines. Tolerance builds quickly and it does nothing about the cause.
Extending time in bed to catch up. It dilutes sleep pressure across more hours and makes tomorrow night worse.
protocols.timeline: Usually worst in weeks 1-2 and resolved for most people by week 4. Past week 4-6 it becomes a prescriber conversation rather than something to wait out.
protocols.source: Stimulus control and sleep restriction are core CBT-I components; the AASM guideline recommends CBT-I as first-line for chronic insomnia ahead of medication. Applying them during antidepressant initiation is standard clinical practice, not a separately trialled protocol. CHANGED: 'tolerance builds within about a week' for antihistamines softened to 'quickly', because the specific one-week figure is commonly repeated but I could not source it.

protocols.bodyEffect: Napping is not forbidden, but a long or late nap spends the sleep pressure you need at 11pm. The rules are about length and timing.
protocols.mechanism: Adenosine accumulates through the waking day and is what eventually makes you fall asleep; a long nap clears a chunk of it, so a 90-minute nap at 5pm can cost you most of the night.
doThis: If you nap: 10-25 minutes, before 3pm, alarm set, and ideally not in your bed.
If you are also fighting insomnia at night, do not nap at all. In that specific situation the nap is the problem, not the relief.
On a heavily sedating drug in week one, a short nap is a sensible coping tool. Phase it out as the sedation eases rather than letting it become the routine.
If you cannot get through the day without a long nap past week 4, raise it. It may be a dose or timing issue.
protocols.timeline: Most people can return to their normal napping habits once night sleep settles, around week 4-6.
protocols.source: The two-process model (homeostatic adenosine pressure plus circadian timing) is established, and the short-nap length and timing rules come from shift-work and aviation research in people not taking antidepressants. Applying them to the initiation period is inference.

protocols.bodyEffect: Most antidepressant sleep disruption is a starting effect, not a permanent one. Knowing the shape of the curve is what gets you past day four.
protocols.mechanism: Receptor systems adapt over weeks; the early disruption reflects an abrupt change in serotonergic and noradrenergic tone that the brain then adjusts to.
doThis: Put day 14 and day 28 in your calendar now. Judge the drug at those points rather than on the worst night.
Write one line a night: hours slept, how you feel out of ten. Depression biases memory towards the bad nights, so you will underestimate your own improvement without a record.
Expect any dose increase to restart a smaller version of the same curve. Knowing that in advance stops it feeling like relapse.
If nothing has moved at all by week 4-6, that is real information for your prescriber, not a personal failure.
protocols.timeline: Typical shape, not a guarantee: insomnia and activation peak weeks 1-2 and are mostly gone by week 4; sedation peaks weeks 1-2 and eases by week 3-4; vivid dreams weeks 1-3, fading by week 4-6. Sexual side effects often do not follow this curve at all.
protocols.source: Sleep-related adverse events in SSRI and SNRI trials cluster in the first weeks and decline thereafter, while polysomnographic REM suppression persists throughout treatment (Wilson & Argyropoulos, Drugs 2005). The week-by-week ranges are a synthesised clinical pattern across drugs and studies, not an output of any single trial. The UI must render them as 'usually' and never as a promise.

protocols.bodyEffect: Twitchy legs at night and a sore jaw in the morning are recognised drug effects, not stress.
protocols.mechanism: Increased serotonergic tone dampens dopaminergic pathways that normally suppress motor activity during sleep, so limb movements and jaw clenching increase.
doThis: Name it to your prescriber rather than living with it. It is recognised and therefore actionable.
If legs are the problem, ask for a ferritin test. Low iron stores make restless legs substantially worse and are common, cheap to check and correctable.
If you are clenching, ask your dentist about a night guard before you crack a tooth. It costs far less than the repair.
If a switch is already on the table for other reasons, it is worth asking whether a non-serotonergic option would be less likely to do this.
protocols.timeline: Can begin within days of starting and, unlike most sleep effects, does not reliably fade with time.
protocols.source: Ferri et al., Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews 2023, meta-analysis of periodic leg movements during sleep with antidepressants (12 studies): large effect for SSRIs and venlafaxine, much smaller or absent for others, with the authors explicitly noting the negative finding for other classes needs better-controlled confirmation. CHANGES: duloxetine removed from the drug list, as it was not among the drugs with the demonstrated effect. The bupropion exception is softened from a flat claim to 'less likely', per the authors' own caveat. Bruxism (jaw clenching) is supported by case series and pharmacovigilance signal, not by this meta-analysis, which measured leg movements only. The ferritin link comes from the general restless legs literature, not from antidepressant-specific trials.

protocols.bodyEffect: Delayed or absent orgasm, lower desire, blunted genital sensation. This is a drug effect on the sexual reflex, not a sign you have stopped caring.
protocols.mechanism: Serotonin acting at 5-HT2A receptors applies a brake to the orgasm reflex and suppresses dopamine, which drives desire; some SSRIs, paroxetine in particular, also reduce nitric oxide signalling, which is what produces genital blood flow.
doThis: Tell your prescriber. This is the most common silent reason people stop their medication, and stopping silently is how relapse happens. There are four or five distinct things to try.
Separate depression from drug. Depression itself flattens libido. If desire is coming back but orgasm has become difficult, delayed or muted, that pattern points at the drug.
Note roughly when it started relative to starting or increasing the dose. It makes the prescriber conversation faster and more specific.
Allow more time and more direct stimulation than you needed before. The threshold has genuinely moved, and treating it as the same body creates a second problem on top of the first.
protocols.timeline: Usually appears within the first 1-2 weeks. Unlike nausea or insomnia, it often does NOT resolve on its own. Waiting it out is a weaker strategy here than anywhere else.
protocols.source: Serretti & Chiesa, J Clin Psychopharmacol 2009;29:259-266: treatment-emergent sexual dysfunction 25.8% to 80.3% across antidepressants, highest with sertraline and venlafaxine, and not significantly different from placebo for bupropion, mirtazapine, agomelatine, amineptine, moclobemide and nefazodone. VERIFIED against the abstract. The spread reflects how studies asked; spontaneous reporting gives far lower rates than direct questioning. Never surface a single headline percentage. The nitric oxide component is mechanistic, strongest for paroxetine, and is not a class-wide measured effect, so the wording was narrowed from 'several SSRIs'.

protocols.bodyEffect: Two behavioural things have trial evidence here: putting sex on the calendar, and exercising shortly before it. They help different parts of the problem.
protocols.mechanism: Acute exercise raises sympathetic nervous system activity, which is a required input for genital arousal, the same activation serotonergic drugs have damped down. Scheduling addresses a different problem: less frequent sex is itself associated with worse function.
doThis: Schedule sexual activity rather than waiting for spontaneous desire. In the trial, scheduling regular sexual activity was what improved orgasm function; exercise added nothing further to that.
Where it fits your life, exercise shortly before sexual activity. That was the arm that improved desire, and global sexual function in the women who had dysfunction at baseline.
Three sessions a week of moderate-to-vigorous exercise, sustained at least three weeks before you judge it. Strength training counts.
Do this alongside the prescriber conversation, not instead of it. Set expectations honestly: satisfaction scores did not move in the trial.
protocols.timeline: The trial used three-week arms. Give it at least that long before drawing conclusions.
protocols.source: MATERIALLY CORRECTED. Lorenz & Meston, Depress Anxiety 2014;31:188-95, randomized crossover, n=52 women. Actual findings: exercise immediately before sexual activity significantly improved desire, and global sexual function in those with baseline dysfunction; scheduling regular sexual activity improved orgasm function and exercise did NOT add to that; neither scheduling nor exercise significantly changed sexual satisfaction. The previous version attributed the orgasm benefit to exercise and claimed a satisfaction benefit that the trial explicitly did not find. Women only; extending the pre-sex timing finding to men is mechanistic inference.

protocols.bodyEffect: There is a real menu here: lower the dose, switch drug, add something, or treat downstream. Most people are never told the menu exists.
protocols.mechanism: Because the effect is driven by serotonergic tone, the options work by lowering that tone, adding back dopaminergic and noradrenergic drive, or restoring nitric oxide-mediated blood flow further down the chain.
doThis: Ask about switching to bupropion or mirtazapine, which showed rates no different from placebo in the largest comparative meta-analysis. Vortioxetine is also often raised as lower-risk, on a smaller evidence base.
Ask about adding bupropion alongside what you already take. This has randomised trial support for improving desire and arousal without stopping your current drug.
For erectile difficulty specifically, ask about sildenafil or tadalafil. This has the strongest evidence of any option here, with separate trial evidence in women.

Ask whether a dose reduction is safe for you. Some people recover function at a lower dose that still treats the depression, but the evidence for this is weak and it is a prescriber decision, never a solo experiment.
avoidThis: Drug holidays, deliberately skipping doses at weekends. It risks discontinuation symptoms and relapse, and it does not work at all for long half-life drugs like fluoxetine.
Stopping abruptly on your own. You get discontinuation symptoms plus relapse risk, and you close off every option above.
protocols.timeline: Switching takes weeks and carries a relapse risk. Add-on strategies usually show within 2-4 weeks. PDE5 inhibitors work the same day.
protocols.source: Nurnberg et al., JAMA 2003;289:56-64: 55% of sildenafil-treated men rated much or very much improved versus 4% on placebo, n=90, SSRI-treated men with depression in remission. VERIFIED. Nurnberg et al., JAMA 2008 showed benefit in women. Bupropion augmentation supported by RCTs including Clayton et al. 2004. Serretti & Chiesa 2009 for comparative rates. CHANGES: the bupropion augmentation dose range '150-300mg' was removed, as dosing belongs to the prescriber and I could not tie a single range to a specific trial; 'improving desire, arousal and orgasm' narrowed to desire and arousal, which is where the augmentation evidence is strongest; the dose-reduction case series numbers (23 of 30) were removed as I could not verify the figures against a primary source, and the direction is stated without them; vortioxetine separated out because its comparative evidence is thinner than bupropion's or mirtazapine's.

protocols.bodyEffect: Coming off or switching brings a sleep flare: intense dreams, broken nights, sometimes brief electric-shock sensations as you drift off.
protocols.mechanism: REM sleep that has been suppressed for months rebounds once the serotonergic brake is removed, returning longer and denser for several nights.
doThis: Taper slowly and in agreement with your prescriber. The size of the rebound tracks how fast the drug level falls.
Expect the flare and schedule around it. Do not begin a taper the week before something that matters to you.
Hold wake time and morning light exposure constant through the taper. During a period when nothing else is stable, they are the only anchor you control.
If the dreams are frightening rather than merely vivid, report it. That is a reason to slow the taper, not something to endure quietly.
avoidThis: Skipping doses as an informal taper. It produces sharp peaks and troughs and a worse rebound than a planned reduction.
Stopping abruptly, particularly on paroxetine or venlafaxine. Short half-life drugs produce the sharpest discontinuation symptoms.
Assuming vivid dreams after a missed dose mean the drug is dangerous. It means the level dropped. Take the next dose on schedule and tell your prescriber if it keeps happening.
protocols.timeline: Begins within days of a reduction or a missed dose and typically peaks over the following 1-2 weeks per step down. Long half-life drugs like fluoxetine produce a delayed and much blunted version of this.
protocols.source: REM rebound after withdrawal of REM-suppressing drugs is established sleep physiology. The week-by-week course during antidepressant tapering is described clinically and in the discontinuation-symptom literature rather than quantified in controlled polysomnography, so the direction is stated confidently and the timings loosely. The half-life-dependent severity of discontinuation symptoms (worst for paroxetine and venlafaxine, mildest for fluoxetine) is well established and was added to avoidThis.

protocols.bodyEffect: Most of your body's serotonin lives in your gut, not your brain. These drugs raise it there first, which is why week one feels like a stomach bug.
protocols.mechanism: The large majority of the body's serotonin sits in the GI tract; blocking reuptake leaves more of it around enterochromaffin cells and vagal nerve endings, where 5-HT3 receptors trigger nausea and 5-HT4 receptors speed the gut up.
doThis: Eat something small 20-30 minutes before your dose, even with zero appetite
Take the dose at the same time daily so you can tell drug effect from random bad days
Score your nausea 0-10 once a day at the same hour, so you can see the slope instead of guessing
eatThis: Plain starch (rice, potato, crackers, toast) which empties fast from a slowed stomach
Cold or room-temperature food, since food aroma is a strong nausea trigger
Broth or salted soup, which replaces fluid and sodium if stools are loose
avoidThis: Judging the drug on day 4, which is usually the worst point rather than the new normal
Alcohol in the first fortnight, which adds gastric irritation and loosens stools on top of the drug effect
protocols.timeline: Starts within the first days and is concentrated in the first two weeks. In pooled vortioxetine trial data, nausea had a median duration of 9-16 days, and only about 2% of patients reported nausea as a NEW symptom during week 3. Brand new nausea appearing after week 2 is uncommon and worth mentioning to your prescriber.
protocols.source: Timeline figures (median duration 9-16 days; ~2% new-onset nausea in week 3) are from the pooled analysis of vortioxetine placebo-controlled RCTs and open-label extensions, PMC4794082, verified directly. The 5-HT3/5-HT4 gut mechanism is established pharmacology. IMPORTANT: the specific tactics here (eating before the dose, fixed dose timing, 0-10 scoring) are general nausea practice and a practical self-tracking method, NOT trial-tested in people starting antidepressants.

protocols.bodyEffect: The nausea tracks how fast your dose climbs, not whether there is food in your stomach. Starting lower is the lever that actually works.
protocols.mechanism: Nausea scales with the size of the serotonin jump at the gut wall, so a smaller starting dose produces a smaller 5-HT3 signal; food alters absorption slightly but does not reduce the serotonergic drive itself.
doThis: Ask your prescriber whether you can start at half the target dose for the first week or two, then step up
If nausea spiked right after a dose increase, ask about dropping back one step and climbing more slowly
Keep taking it with food if that feels better to you, it is harmless, just do not expect it to be the fix
avoidThis: Assuming food will solve it, then concluding the drug is intolerable when food does not work
Pushing the dose up faster than planned to get the adjustment over with
Splitting or crushing extended-release SNRI capsules to lower the dose without asking, which dumps the whole dose at once
protocols.timeline: Dose-related nausea appears within days of each increase and settles over roughly a week once the dose holds steady.
protocols.source: Randomised 4-arm trial of duloxetine initiation, n=249 (30 mg vs 60 mg, each with vs without food), PMC3521117, verified directly: dose effect on nausea severity p=0.003; food effect p=0.555 (not significant); ~80% on 30 mg had no or mild nausea in week 1 vs ~55% on 60 mg. THREE LIMITS the app should not hide: (1) the trial was OPEN-LABEL, which the authors flag as a source of expectation bias; (2) it was conducted in Korean patients and the authors explicitly raise diet and ethnicity as reasons their food result may differ from Western populations; (3) all arms escalated to 60 mg at week 1, so this tests the STARTING dose, not maintenance. Extending the dose-over-food finding from duloxetine to the other drugs listed is mechanistic inference, not tested.

protocols.bodyEffect: Food helps a raw, burning stomach. It does much less for the deep queasy wave, which is nerve signalling rather than stomach contents.
protocols.mechanism: Food buffers direct contact irritation between the tablet and the stomach lining, but 5-HT3-mediated nausea is generated by vagal nerve signalling from the gut wall and is largely independent of whether the stomach is full.
doThis: Sort your symptom first: burning, sour or reflux-like means food and staying upright 30 minutes will genuinely help
Deep queasy waves with no burning means food is optional, so choose dose timing by sleep instead
If the queasiness peaks a few hours after dosing, try taking it at bedtime so you sleep through the peak
If it wakes you or wrecks your sleep, move it to morning with breakfast instead
eatThis: A small starch-plus-protein pairing such as toast with egg, or crackers with yogurt
avoidThis: Force-feeding yourself a large meal to soak up the tablet, which slows gastric emptying and usually worsens queasiness
protocols.timeline: You will know within 3-4 days whether food is doing anything for you. If it is not, stop treating it as the solution and address dose timing instead.
protocols.source: The null food effect is trial-based (duloxetine RCT, PMC3521117, food p=0.555, verified). Sorting nausea by subtype and matching food to gastric irritation specifically is mechanistic reasoning, NOT a tested strategy. Supporting PK point, verified against the FDA Zoloft label: for the sertraline TABLET, food raised Cmax by 25% and shortened Tmax from 8 to 5.5 hours, so food does not lower systemic exposure. Note this is formulation-specific: for the ORAL CONCENTRATE the label reports Tmax lengthening from 5.9 to 7.0 hours with food, the opposite direction. Do not present the tablet figure as applying to all sertraline forms, or to other drugs.

protocols.bodyEffect: Ginger's active compounds act on the same 5-HT3 receptors your drug is over-stimulating. Worth trying, modest at best, and never tested for this exact use.
protocols.mechanism: Gingerols and shogaols have inhibitory activity at 5-HT3, muscarinic and histaminergic receptors and modestly accelerate gastric emptying, which overlaps the pathway 5-HT3 anti-sickness drugs work on.
doThis: Aim for around 1000 mg of ginger daily, which is the dose most trials used
Start it on day 1 of the antidepressant rather than waiting until you already feel awful
Use capsules, fresh root steeped in hot water, or crystallised ginger, not ginger ale or ginger biscuits, which contain little real ginger
Expect help with queasiness rather than with actual vomiting, which is where the evidence is null
eatThis: Ginger capsules
Fresh ginger steeped in hot water, which also covers fluid intake
Crystallised ginger for a portable option between meals
avoidThis: Going above about 1500 mg a day, since subgroup analysis favoured lower daily doses and higher intake adds side effects rather than benefit
Ginger supplements without checking first if you take warfarin or another anticoagulant, or have surgery coming up, because concentrated ginger at high doses can raise bleeding risk
protocols.timeline: Trials generally dosed it daily for around 4 days and measured over days, not hours. Worth using consistently through the first 2-3 weeks, then stopping to see if you still need it.
protocols.source: DOWNGRADED from clinical_studies. Real RCTs exist but NONE in antidepressant-induced nausea, so the recommendation itself rests on shared-receptor extrapolation. Verified directly (Nutrition Journal 2014 meta-analysis, PMC3995184, 12 RCTs / 1,278 pregnant women): ginger significantly reduced nausea severity vs placebo (MD 1.20, 95% CI 0.56-1.84, p=0.0002, I-squared 0%) but did NOT significantly reduce vomiting episodes (MD 0.72, 95% CI -0.03 to 1.46, p=0.06). Most trials used 1000 mg/day for 4 days; subgroup analysis favoured <1500 mg/day. Chemotherapy-nausea evidence is weaker and largely null. REMOVED from the previous draft: the '250 mg four times daily' split (no trial used that schedule) and the '30-60 minute onset' claim (not in any source checked).

protocols.bodyEffect: Extra gut serotonin hits 5-HT4 receptors, which speed the colon up. Stool moves too fast for water to be reabsorbed, so it comes out loose.
protocols.mechanism: Blocking the serotonin transporter raises local gut serotonin, which activates 5-HT4 receptors on enteric neurons, increases acetylcholine release and drives colonic propulsion, cutting the time available for water absorption.
doThis: Start psyllium husk, 1 teaspoon in a full large glass of water once daily, and build up gradually over a week
Cut caffeine right down in the first fortnight, since caffeine independently stimulates colonic contractions and stacks with the drug effect
Replace fluid with something containing salt (broth, oral rehydration sachets, salted soup) rather than plain water alone if stools are frequent
If it is severe, ask your prescriber about switching, since this differs a lot between drugs in the same class
eatThis: Psyllium husk, which forms a gel that traps excess water and firms stool
Oats and ripe banana as soluble-fibre foods
White rice and potato, which are low-residue and slow transit
avoidThis: Wheat bran or generic advice to add more roughage, because coarse insoluble fibre mechanically stimulates mucosal secretion and can make loose stools worse
Taking psyllium with too little water, which is the usual reason people find it unpleasant and quit
Sugar alcohols (sorbitol, xylitol in sugar-free gum and sweets) and a big lactose load while this is settling
protocols.timeline: Often lags the nausea. Can appear in the first weeks. Note the source meta-analysis measured outcomes at around 8 weeks and does NOT report how these symptoms evolve over time, so any specific 'settles by week X' figure for diarrhoea would be invented.
protocols.source: Network and dose-response meta-analysis of antidepressant GI effects (Transl Psychiatry 2025, PMC12811249), verified directly. Diarrhoea ORs vs placebo, all significant: vilazodone 3.88 (2.69-5.64), fluvoxamine 3.15 (1.30-7.59), sertraline 2.90 (2.23-3.74), citalopram 2.60 (1.53-4.47), agomelatine 2.17 (1.09-4.47), fluoxetine 1.95 (1.56-2.44), escitalopram 1.87 (1.36-2.66), paroxetine 1.62 (1.34-1.97). DRUG LIST CORRECTED: venlafaxine and desvenlafaxine were REMOVED because they are NOT among the 8 drugs with significantly increased diarrhoea odds; paroxetine was ADDED because it is (weakest signal, and note paroxetine also raises constipation risk, so it can go either way in different people). The 5-HT4 mechanism is established pharmacology. The psyllium-versus-wheat-bran claim is presented as direction only; the specific trial citation in the previous draft was not verified in this pass and has been removed.

protocols.bodyEffect: Paroxetine blocks acetylcholine; SNRIs add noradrenaline. Both slow the gut. Unlike nausea, there is no known mechanism that rescues you from this one with time.
protocols.mechanism: Muscarinic receptor blockade by paroxetine inhibits smooth muscle contraction and prolongs transit, and noradrenergic tone from SNRIs slows gastric emptying. Neither pathway has the receptor desensitisation that turns down 5-HT3 nausea. Fluvoxamine carries the highest constipation odds of the drugs here despite not being strongly anticholinergic, which is not well explained.
doThis: Treat it from week 1 rather than waiting it out
Soluble fibre plus genuinely increased fluid, since fibre without fluid makes constipation worse
Ask about polyethylene glycol (macrogol) as the first-line agent rather than stimulant laxatives for ongoing use
Walk after meals, which uses the gastrocolic reflex while it is active

If it is persistent and intolerable, ask about switching: vortioxetine, fluoxetine, sertraline, citalopram and escitalopram were the only drugs in the meta-analysis with no significant constipation increase
eatThis: Psyllium husk with a large glass of water, which softens hard stool as well as firming loose stool
Kiwi fruit, prunes or pears as sources of both fibre and sorbitol
avoidThis: Assuming the 'give it two weeks and it settles' advice transfers from nausea to constipation, since nothing in the evidence base supports that transfer
Long-term daily stimulant laxatives without discussing it with a clinician
protocols.timeline: Builds over the first weeks. Whether it persists for the duration of treatment is NOT established: the meta-analysis measured constipation at around 8 weeks and does not report symptom trajectory at all.
protocols.source: DOWNGRADED from clinical_studies. The drug attributions ARE trial-derived, but the protocol's headline claim (that constipation does not settle) has NO trial support: PMC12811249 was checked directly and reports no data on duration, tolerance or trajectory. The absence-of-desensitisation argument is inference from contrast with 5-HT3 nausea. Verified constipation ORs vs placebo: fluvoxamine 4.00 (1.37-12.5), venlafaxine 3.19 (2.41-4.30), paroxetine 2.38 (1.92-2.99), desvenlafaxine 2.35 (1.36-4.25), duloxetine 2.33 (1.71-3.17); higher still for amitriptyline 4.47, clomipramine 4.33, reboxetine 4.02, levomilnacipran 3.77. Verbatim: 'With the exception of vortioxetine, fluoxetine, sertraline, citalopram and escitalopram, all drugs demonstrated a greater incidence of constipation in comparison to the placebo.' DRUG LIST CORRECTED: fluvoxamine was ADDED (it was missing, despite having the highest constipation OR of any in-scope drug, though with a wide credible interval). The unverified secondary review cited in the previous draft has been removed.

protocols.bodyEffect: A nauseated stomach empties slowly. Large meals sit and make it worse; small frequent ones hold blood sugar without overloading it.
protocols.mechanism: Nausea and raised serotonin both slow gastric emptying, so a large volume stays in the stomach longer and distends it, which is itself a nausea trigger via the same vagal afferents.
doThis: Eat 5-6 small meals rather than 3 normal ones for the first fortnight
Get 25-30 g of protein at breakfast (2 eggs plus Greek yogurt, or a scoop of whey in oats) to protect muscle while intake is down
Drink to thirst in modest amounts rather than large glasses at once, since a full stomach distends and triggers nausea. Keep your total daily fluid roughly normal, not elevated
If you are drinking more than usual because of loose stools or vomiting, make some of it salt-containing (broth, oral rehydration sachet) rather than all plain water
Switch to liquid calories (smoothie, milk, soup) on days solid food is unbearable, rather than eating nothing
eatThis: Greek yogurt, eggs, oats, crackers with nut butter as small protein-containing units
Cold or room-temperature food, which gives off far less aroma
Broth and salted soup, covering fluid and sodium together
avoidThis: Skipping meals all day then eating one large evening meal, which is the worst possible pattern for a slow stomach
Hot, strongly aromatic food, because smell drives nausea more than taste does
Deliberately pushing large volumes of plain water to 'flush out' the nausea. On these drugs that is not neutral: it can worsen dilutional low sodium. See the low-sodium protocol
Alcohol, which irritates the stomach lining and loosens stools independently
protocols.timeline: Use this pattern for the first 2-3 weeks, then return to normal meals as nausea recedes.
protocols.source: Standard nausea-management practice plus established physiology of delayed gastric emptying, applied to antidepressant start-up. Not trial-tested in this population. The 25-30 g protein target reflects general protein-distribution guidance for preserving lean mass during reduced intake, not an antidepressant-specific study. SAFETY CORRECTION: the previous draft instructed '150-200 ml of fluid every 30-60 minutes', which at the upper bound is roughly 5-6 litres a day across waking hours. That was an invented number and it points in exactly the wrong direction for a drug class that causes SIADH and dilutional hyponatraemia. Replaced with drink-to-thirst plus salt-containing replacement, and cross-referenced to the low-sodium protocol.

protocols.bodyEffect: Early appetite loss is drug-driven, not just low mood. It is best documented for fluoxetine and duloxetine.
protocols.mechanism: Serotonin acting at 5-HT2C receptors reduces food intake, and nausea suppresses appetite on top of that. Both effects are strongest in the first weeks, before receptor adaptation.
doThis: Eat by the clock, not by hunger, because the hunger signal itself is being suppressed
Prioritise 25-30 g protein at breakfast so the weight you lose is not muscle
Use liquid calories when solid food repels you, since a smoothie is far easier than a plate
Weigh yourself weekly under the same conditions rather than daily, so you see trend not noise
eatThis: Whole milk, nut butters and olive oil as easy calorie density without volume
Whey or milk-based smoothies, which deliver protein without needing appetite
Greek yogurt and eggs as small high-protein units
avoidThis: Treating it as a welcome side effect and eating less on purpose, because the appetite suppression reverses and low protein intake means you lose lean mass rather than fat
Ignoring loss above roughly 5% of body weight in a month, which should be flagged to your prescriber
protocols.timeline: Appetite suppression is strongest in the first weeks. In the 1-year fluoxetine trial, mean weight change over the first 4 weeks was -0.4 kg, then reversed.
protocols.source: Michelson et al., Changes in Weight During a 1-Year Trial of Fluoxetine, Am J Psychiatry 1999;156(8):1170, verified: mean absolute decrease of 0.4 kg over the first 4 weeks of therapy, reversing thereafter. Decreased appetite is listed as a common adverse reaction in duloxetine labelling. DRUG LIST CORRECTED: the previous draft applied this to all ten drugs and specifically included PAROXETINE, which is the SSRI most associated with weight GAIN, i.e. the opposite direction. Scoped back to the two drugs with actual supporting evidence. The specific '>5% and at least twice placebo rate' label figure for duloxetine could not be confirmed in this pass and has been removed. The 5% body weight in a month escalation threshold is a general clinical malnutrition-screening convention, not an antidepressant-specific finding. Protein and liquid-calorie tactics are extrapolated nutrition practice.

protocols.bodyEffect: Appetite returns over the following months, sometimes sharply. Partly recovery from depression, partly receptors adapting.
protocols.mechanism: Sustained 5-HT2C stimulation is thought to desensitise and downregulate those receptors, releasing the early appetite brake, while recovering mood independently restores normal eating and interest in food.
doThis: Expect regain back toward your baseline and do not read it as the drug failing or as relapse
Keep the protein-forward breakfast you built in the first month, since it blunts later-day appetite swings
Build a walking or activity habit during month 2, before appetite fully returns, so it is already established
If weight gain is steady and unwanted past month 6, raise it as a medication-choice question rather than a willpower question
avoidThis: Sharp calorie restriction the moment appetite returns, which tends to backfire while mood is still stabilising
protocols.timeline: In the 1-year fluoxetine trial, early loss reversed after about 4 weeks, and patients completing 50 weeks gained a mean of roughly 3 kg during continuation, with no significant difference between fluoxetine and placebo.
protocols.source: Michelson et al., Am J Psychiatry 1999;156(8):1170, verified: continuation-phase weight gain (~3 kg over 50 weeks) matched placebo and was attributed to recovery from depression rather than to the drug. The 5-HT2C desensitisation account is the standard mechanistic explanation but was NOT measured in these patients; it is inference. This pattern is documented for FLUOXETINE; do not present it as class-wide. Paroxetine in particular is more associated with longer-term gain, so the reassuring 'same as placebo' framing should not be shown to paroxetine users without that caveat.

protocols.bodyEffect: Vortioxetine causes nausea in roughly one in four people, despite blocking 5-HT3 receptors. Rates are higher at higher doses.
protocols.mechanism: Vortioxetine blocks 5-HT3 receptors, which was expected to spare people nausea, but its serotonin reuptake inhibition raises gut serotonin enough that meaningful nausea rates remain.
doThis: If you started at 10 mg and are struggling, ask about 5 mg for the first two weeks before stepping up
Front-load your nausea support (ginger, small frequent meals) in the first fortnight, which is when almost all of it happens
If nausea is still bad after several weeks, raise it with your prescriber rather than continuing to endure it
avoidThis: Assuming that because you tolerated a lower dose, a higher one will be equally easy: nausea rates and nausea-related discontinuation are both higher at 15-20 mg than at 5-10 mg
protocols.timeline: Onset is early and most nausea falls in the first two weeks, with a median duration of 9-16 days. By week 3, only about 2% of patients report nausea as a new symptom.
protocols.source: Pooled analysis of vortioxetine randomised placebo-controlled trials and open-label extensions (PMC4794082), verified directly. Nausea by dose: placebo 8.1%, 5 mg 20.9%, 10 mg 23.3%, 15 mg 31.2%, 20 mg 27.8%. Discontinuation due to nausea: placebo 0.3%, 5 mg 1.2%, 10 mg 1.5%, 15 mg 3.8%, 20 mg 3.6%. Short-term weight change -0.1 to +0.1 kg with no dose-related trend; 0.7-0.8 kg gain over 52 weeks. THREE CORRECTIONS: (1) the previous draft called the dose-response 'clear' and said rates rise with dose, but the data are NOT monotonic (15 mg 31.2% exceeds 20 mg 27.8%, and the same inversion appears in discontinuation) so this is now stated as higher-band vs lower-band; (2) the claim that 'up to 20% report nausea within 2 days' was checked against the source and is NOT there, removed; (3) the claim that 'roughly 10% on 10-20 mg still have nausea at 6-8 weeks' is NOT in the source either (the paper reports whole-period incidence and does not disaggregate by endpoint) so it was removed along with the 'you are in the persistent subgroup at week 6' advice built on it. The comparison 'nausea rates end up similar to duloxetine' was also unsourced and removed.

protocols.bodyEffect: Settling means fewer bad hours per day, even if the bad hours are still bad. Not settling means the weekly average is flat or rising.
protocols.mechanism: 5-HT3 receptors desensitise under continuous stimulation, turning down the emetic signal over 1-2 weeks. Where that desensitisation is going to happen, it tends to show as a downward slope well before symptoms fully stop.
doThis: Score nausea 0-10 once daily at a fixed time and compare week-on-week averages, not day-to-day
By day 10-14, look for a downward slope; the absolute number matters less than the direction
Contact your prescriber if the average is flat or rising at day 14, rather than waiting to hit a month
If GI symptoms are unchanged at 3-4 weeks despite a dose adjustment, treat that as a conversation about changing something rather than a reason to keep waiting
avoidThis: Judging on single bad days, which is how most people abandon a drug that was actually working

Stopping abruptly, especially paroxetine and venlafaxine, whose short half-lives produce discontinuation symptoms that include their own nausea and can be mistaken for the original side effect. Any stopping or switching decision goes through your prescriber
Assuming constipation follows the same settling curve as nausea
protocols.timeline: Nausea is concentrated in the first two weeks (median duration 9-16 days in pooled vortioxetine data, ~2% new onset by week 3). The 3-4 week point is a reasonable review threshold rather than a guideline-mandated one.
protocols.source: DOWNGRADED from guideline. The previous draft marked this 'guideline' but the underlying citation was a secondary educational review, not a named clinical guideline from a body such as NICE or APA, and that review was not verified in this pass. The nausea time course IS trial-based (PMC4794082, verified). The 3-4 week decision threshold and the 0-10 daily scoring method are practical framing, not a validated instrument and not a sourced guideline recommendation. The 5-HT3 desensitisation account is established pharmacology but the inference that a visible downward slope predicts eventual resolution is reasoning, not a measured predictor.

protocols.bodyEffect: A few people develop low blood sodium, which feels like start-up nausea with headache and fog added. It is uncommon, but it does not only happen in the first fortnight.
protocols.mechanism: These drugs can trigger inappropriate antidiuretic hormone release, so the kidneys retain water and dilute blood sodium. Low sodium itself causes nausea, appetite loss, headache and confusion.
doThis: If your nausea comes with headache, confusion, unsteadiness, muscle cramps or unusual drowsiness, ask for a sodium blood test rather than assuming it is normal start-up
Be more alert to this if you are over 65, female, of low body weight, or taking a diuretic, which are the consistently reported risk factors
Mention any diuretic you take when starting, since older adults on an SSRI plus a diuretic are the highest-risk group by a wide margin
Keep this on your list even months in, not just during the first fortnight
avoidThis: Drinking very large volumes of plain water to flush the nausea if these features are present, since that can worsen dilutional low sodium
Dismissing new confusion or unsteadiness in an older person as depression or as the drug settling in
Assuming you are past the risk window once the start-up nausea has gone
protocols.timeline: Reported median onset is around 13-14 days, but the documented range runs from 1 day to over 250 days, and about 29% of cases are diagnosed more than 3 months after starting. The early cluster overlaps the normal start-up nausea window, which is why it gets missed there, but a late presentation is not rare.
protocols.source: Observational case-control and case-series literature on antidepressant-associated hyponatraemia and SIADH (including PMC1874265, checked directly). Reported relative risks: SSRIs ~3.9-fold vs other antidepressants; paroxetine ~5.1-fold; age 65+ ~6.3-fold; elderly patients on an SSRI plus a diuretic ~13.5-fold. These are observational, not trial, estimates. TIMING CORRECTED: the previous draft stated 'median onset around 9 days, typically within the first 1-14 days'. That figure was not supported by the sources checked, which put the median nearer 13-14 days, and more importantly the '1-14 days' framing implies an all-clear at two weeks that the data contradict, since roughly one in three cases present after 3 months. This mattered because the protocol's whole purpose is helping someone notice a symptom they would otherwise dismiss. Frame as a discrimination check, not an expected event.

protocols.bodyEffect: Serotonin is what platelets use to clot. These drugs deplete it, so bleeding risk rises, especially alongside ibuprofen.
protocols.mechanism: Platelets cannot make their own serotonin and take it up through the same transporter these drugs block, so platelet serotonin falls and clotting is impaired. NSAIDs simultaneously strip the stomach's protective prostaglandin layer.
doThis: Use paracetamol or acetaminophen for the start-up headache rather than ibuprofen, naproxen or aspirin
If you need regular NSAIDs for a pain condition, ask about a stomach-protecting drug such as a proton pump inhibitor
Tell your prescriber about aspirin, anticoagulants or regular anti-inflammatories before you start
avoidThis: Reaching for ibuprofen by default for the headache that often accompanies the first fortnight
Combining NSAIDs with alcohol while on these drugs
Ignoring black tarry stool or vomit that looks like coffee grounds, which need urgent medical attention rather than a wait-and-see
protocols.timeline: Risk is present from the start and continues throughout treatment. It does not settle the way nausea does.
protocols.source: SSRI and SNRI product labelling carries a bleeding-risk warning covering concomitant NSAIDs, aspirin, warfarin and other anticoagulants; this is standard labelled content across the class (FDA Zoloft label, accessdata.fda.gov). The platelet serotonin depletion mechanism is well-established pharmacology. Note: in this pass I verified the Zoloft label's pharmacokinetics section directly but did not independently re-fetch the warnings section, so if the app displays label text verbatim it should be pulled from the current label rather than paraphrased from here. No risk magnitude is quoted because I did not source one; direction only.

protocols.bodyEffect: Your platelets can't restock their serotonin, so clots form a little slower. Bruises spread further and small cuts ooze for longer.
protocols.mechanism: Platelets cannot manufacture serotonin — they load it from the blood using the same transporter your medication blocks, so platelet serotonin content falls substantially (studies report reductions in the range of 65-90% versus controls after some weeks), and the burst of serotonin that normally clamps down the vessel and recruits more platelets at an injury site is much weaker.
doThis: Expect more bruising and slower-stopping nosebleeds and gum bleeds. On its own this is a nuisance, not a danger — in a low-risk population the number needed to harm for one extra upper-GI bleed was around 3,200 people treated, so roughly one in three thousand.
Reach for paracetamol/acetaminophen instead of ibuprofen, naproxen or aspirin for everyday aches. It does nothing to platelets or stomach lining.
If you need an anti-inflammatory for a joint or muscle, ask about a topical NSAID gel — far less of it reaches the bloodstream than with tablets.
Tell your dentist and any surgeon which antidepressant you take. Nobody usually stops it, but they plan differently.
avoidThis: Regular ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac or daily aspirin alongside your antidepressant without discussing it — this specific pairing is where the risk actually lives, not in the antidepressant by itself.
Ignoring black tarry stools, vomit that looks like coffee grounds, or blood in vomit or stool. These are emergency signs, not wait-and-see signs.
Assuming this is permanent if you come off — platelet serotonin is expected to refill as platelets turn over, over roughly two weeks after stopping.
protocols.timeline: Platelet serotonin falls over the first weeks of treatment and stays low the whole time you take the drug; it is expected to refill over roughly 2 weeks after stopping, in line with platelet turnover
protocols.source: Mechanism and platelet serotonin depletion range (65-90% versus controls after weeks of treatment): Bixby, VandenBerg & Bostwick, 'Clinical Management of Bleeding Risk With Antidepressants', Ann Pharmacother 2019, and the operative-bleeding review literature. Risk figures: Anglin et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2014;109(6):811-819 — SSRI alone OR 1.66 (95% CI 1.44-1.92) in case-control studies; NNH 3,177 (95% CI 2,279-4,765) in a low-risk Dutch population, 881 (95% CI 632-1,321) in a higher-risk US cohort. The absolute-risk framing is derived from that NNH, not from a guideline. The 2-week refill after stopping is inferred from platelet lifespan, not measured in a dedicated trial.

protocols.bodyEffect: Ibuprofen strips the stomach's protective lining while your antidepressant slows clotting. Two separate injuries landing on the same spot.
protocols.mechanism: NSAIDs block prostaglandins that maintain the gastric mucus barrier, creating small erosions; your antidepressant separately removes the platelet serotonin needed to seal them. The observed risk for the combination is well above what either does alone, which is consistent with the two injuries compounding rather than simply adding.
doThis: Default to paracetamol/acetaminophen for headaches, period pain and general aches. For most everyday pain it is genuinely adequate.
Check cold and flu combination sachets and back-pain tablets — many quietly contain ibuprofen or aspirin. Read the active ingredients, not the brand name.

If you have a condition that genuinely needs regular NSAIDs (arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis), ask your prescriber about adding a proton pump inhibitor. Gastroprotection is standard for higher-risk NSAID users and this combination is a reasonable candidate for it.
If you also take an anticoagulant such as warfarin, apixaban or rivaroxaban, flag the antidepressant explicitly. Risk was highest in the first 30 days of the two being taken together.
avoidThis: Low-dose daily aspirin taken 'for the heart' without a doctor having actually recommended it — the bleeding arithmetic changes once you are on a serotonergic antidepressant.
Treating a hangover with ibuprofen. Alcohol thins the mucus layer too, so that is three hits at once.
protocols.timeline: Risk is present from the first co-administered dose; it does not build up or wear off with time on the antidepressant
protocols.source: Anglin et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2014;109(6):811-819: upper-GI bleeding with concurrent SSRI + NSAID OR 4.25 (95% CI 2.82-6.42). Other meta-analyses report substantially higher point estimates (Bixby et al. 2019 cite an across-study OR range of roughly 3.2-10.9), so the direction is consistent but the magnitude is not well pinned down and no single number should be presented as the answer. Anticoagulants: Rahman et al., JAMA Netw Open 2024 — nested case-control in UK atrial fibrillation patients, ~33% increased major bleeding when an SSRI was added to an oral anticoagulant, strongest in the first 30 days and substantially attenuated after 6 months. PPI gastroprotection is a general NSAID-risk guideline position extended to this pairing by inference, not a trial result in SSRI users.

protocols.bodyEffect: Your kidneys hold on to too much water, diluting the salt in your blood. This is water excess, not salt loss — and that difference changes the fix.
protocols.mechanism: Serotonin signalling increases release of antidiuretic hormone, so the kidney keeps reabsorbing free water it should be passing; the total sodium in your body is roughly normal, it is just spread through too much fluid.
doThis: Drink to thirst, normally. That is the whole instruction. Water is the thing being retained, so more of it makes the number worse, not better.
Salt your food as you normally would. Do not go low-salt unnecessarily during the first month.

Know the early signs, because they are cruelly easy to mistake for ordinary start-up side effects: headache, nausea, feeling unsteady or off-balance, unusual tiredness, muscle cramps, confusion or trouble concentrating. The discriminator is direction: start-up effects improve into week three, this gets worse. Worsening is the signal to get a blood test.
If you are over 65, on a thiazide or loop diuretic, low body weight, female, or have had low sodium before, ask for a sodium check in the first few weeks. Most cases show up in that window.
eatThis: Normal salted food, soups and broths — not as treatment, just don't restrict salt while your body is already diluting it
avoidThis: Drinking large amounts of water to 'flush out' the nausea or to be healthy. This is the single most common way people make hyponatraemia worse, and the instinct is completely understandable.
Taking salt tablets or electrolyte sachets to self-correct without a blood test — you cannot tell from symptoms whether you are low, and correcting sodium too fast has its own serious risks.
Restricting your fluid on your own initiative. Fluid restriction is the standard treatment, but it is a decision that needs an actual sodium result behind it, not a guess.
Endurance exercise in hot weather with heavy plain-water intake during the first month.
MDMA, which causes both water retention and heavy water drinking, and has caused severe hyponatraemia in people on SSRIs.
protocols.timeline: Usually shows up in the first 2-4 weeks, most often within the first 2; risk drops after the first month; sodium typically normalises 2-20 days after stopping the drug
protocols.source: Hyponatraemia/SIADH is a labelled warning for SSRIs, SNRIs and mirtazapine. Onset typically within the first 2 weeks, and normalisation 2-20 days after discontinuation, come from the review literature (e.g. De Picker et al., Psychosomatics 2014, class-by-class review) — observational, not trial-derived. Risk factors (older age, female sex, diuretic co-prescription, low body weight, low baseline sodium) come from observational cohorts and case-control studies, so ranking is associational. The frequently quoted diuretic figure (OR 13.5) has a 95% CI of 1.8-101 and is far too imprecise to quote as a number to patients — it is reported here only as 'diuretics raise the risk'. Mirtazapine: Ramos et al., systematic review 2022 (pooled incidence ~3.3%, mean onset ~34 days). The 'drink to thirst, do not water-load' advice follows from SIADH being water excess and from fluid restriction being first-line treatment — standard practice, stated as mechanism, not as a trial result.

protocols.bodyEffect: Bone-building and bone-clearing cells both carry serotonin transporters, so bone turnover may shift slightly across years of treatment. How much this matters in a real skeleton is genuinely unresolved.
protocols.mechanism: Osteoblasts and osteoclasts express the same serotonin transporter your medication blocks, and in human cell culture SSRIs inhibited the formation and function of both. The concentrations used were micromolar, above typical plasma levels — though SSRIs are known to concentrate in bone marrow above blood levels, so the gap between dish and skeleton is not as clean as it first looks in either direction.
doThis: Do something weight-bearing and something resistance-based. Loading the skeleton is the intervention with the best evidence here — resistance training combined with impact (jumping, hopping, stair climbing, brisk walking) is what actually moves bone density in trials.
Get calcium from food rather than a pill where you can. Guideline intakes sit around 1000-1200mg per day for adults at risk.
Keep vitamin D adequate if you are deficient — typically 800-1000 IU per day. This is for bone and muscle, not for mood.
If you are postmenopausal, over 65, on long-term steroids, or have a fracture history, ask whether a DEXA scan is warranted. The SSRI is one input into that decision, not the whole decision.
eatThis: Tinned sardines or salmon eaten with the soft bones — one of the densest calcium sources there is, and it brings omega-3 with it
Kale, pak choi and broccoli — calcium from these is absorbed well because they are low in oxalate, unlike spinach where oxalate binds the calcium up
Milk or fortified soya/oat milk, roughly 240mg calcium per 200ml glass
Protein at each meal — bone matrix is largely collagen, and low protein intake tracks with lower bone density
avoidThis: Treating a calcium supplement as a substitute for loading the skeleton. A 2026 BMJ meta-analysis of 69 randomised trials in 153,902 adults found calcium and/or vitamin D supplements gave no clinically meaningful fracture or fall reduction in community-dwelling older adults. Correcting a real dietary or vitamin D deficiency is a different question from supplementing on top of adequacy — but the mechanical loading is the part doing the work.
Smoking and heavy alcohol, both of which suppress osteoblast activity directly and stack on top of this.

Panicking about it. Some share of the observed fracture excess in SSRI users is likely falls — from dizziness, sedation and low sodium — rather than fragile bone, and depression itself independently tracks with lower bone density.
protocols.timeline: This is a years-long association, not a weeks-long one; nothing measurable changes in your skeleton in the first months of treatment
protocols.source: This is the weakest-evidence item in this set and is labelled accordingly. Receptor biology: 'Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors Inhibit Human Osteoclast and Osteoblast Formation and Function', Biological Psychiatry 2012 — human cell culture, micromolar concentrations; the same paper notes SSRIs sequester in bone marrow at higher concentrations than blood or brain. I have removed a previously stated claim that citalopram was the exception, as I could not verify it in the source. Clinical association: Diem et al. and related prospective cohorts reporting faster annual hip bone loss in SSRI users than non-users — observational and heavily confounded by depression itself, inactivity, smoking and falls; I have removed the previously quoted '1.6-fold' multiplier as I could not confirm the exact figure. No trial shows that any intervention prevents SSRI-associated bone loss specifically. The exercise and calcium/vitamin D advice is borrowed from general bone-health evidence (resistance-plus-impact training meta-analyses; Massé et al., BMJ 2026 supplement meta-analysis) and applied here by inference.

protocols.bodyEffect: Exercise reaches depression through routes your tablet doesn't. In trials, arms that combined exercise with an SSRI showed a moderate benefit against control.
protocols.mechanism: Exercise raises BDNF and hippocampal neuroplasticity, damps down inflammatory cytokine signalling, and restores circadian and sleep architecture — pathways only partly overlapping with monoamine reuptake inhibition. That partial non-overlap is the plausible reason it adds something on top, though this mechanistic account is inference, not something the trials measured.
doThis: Pick strength training or yoga if the problem is that you cannot make yourself keep going. These two had the lowest dropout of any modality in the largest network meta-analysis — not because they work better, but because people actually stay in them.

Pick walking or jogging if you want the largest measured effect. Walking or jogging showed the biggest reduction in depression scores versus active control (Hedges' g -0.62, 95% CrI -0.80 to -0.45), with yoga -0.55 and strength training -0.49 close behind.

Start at a size that feels almost embarrassing — ten minutes, once. You are not failing by doing a small amount, and the difference between modalities is smaller than the difference between doing something and doing nothing.

Work harder over time if and when you can. Effects in that analysis were broadly proportional to intensity, so more vigorous exercise tended to do more — but lighter activity still showed benefit. There is no threshold you have to clear to get something.
avoidThis: Waiting to feel motivated. In depression the motivation reliably arrives after the movement, not before it — anhedonia blunts anticipatory reward but leaves consummatory reward more intact, so the wanting comes back once you have started.
Treating this as a replacement for medication. The evidence here is for exercise added to treatment or compared against control, and it was studied that way.
protocols.timeline: Trials mostly ran 8-12 weeks; expect a shift over weeks, not days
protocols.source: Noetel et al., 'Effect of exercise for depression: systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials', BMJ 2024;384:e075847 — 218 studies, 495 arms, 14,170 participants. Versus active control: walking/jogging g -0.62 (95% CrI -0.80 to -0.45), yoga -0.55, strength training -0.49, mixed aerobic -0.43, tai chi/qigong -0.42; exercise combined with SSRIs g -0.55; strength training and yoga had the lowest dropout. I have REMOVED the previously quoted intensity figures (vigorous g -0.74, light g -0.58) and the '10-week versus 30-week' duration claim, as I could not verify either in the source; the paper's verifiable statement is that effects were proportional to intensity, so that is all that is claimed now. CAVEAT the app should surface next to any number: the authors rated confidence in the evidence as low for walking/jogging and very low for most other comparisons under CINeMA, because exercise trials cannot be blinded and small-trial effects are likely. Direction well supported; magnitudes indicative only. The motivation-follows-action point is behavioural activation theory, i.e. mechanistic inference, not a finding of this paper.

protocols.bodyEffect: EPA is built into cell membranes and quiets inflammatory signalling. Low-grade inflammation is one of the routes into depression, though not everyone's route.
protocols.mechanism: EPA competes with arachidonic acid as a substrate, shifting eicosanoid production toward less inflammatory species and lowering cytokines like IL-6 and TNF-alpha — which matters because a subgroup of depression runs with raised inflammatory markers. Whether that is why it helps the people it helps is unproven.
doThis: If you try this, get the composition right, because it is where most people go wrong: you want EPA-predominant, meaning EPA is at least 60% of the total omega-3.

Aim for 1-2g of net EPA per day, as guideline consensus suggests. Read the back of the bottle, not the front — a capsule advertised as '1000mg fish oil' often contains only a couple of hundred mg of EPA, so you would need several. A concentrated EPA product gets you there in one or two.
Give it at least 8 weeks before judging. Benefits in trials emerged over 8-12 weeks.
Treat it as an add-on to your medication, not instead of it. The adjunct evidence is considerably stronger than the monotherapy evidence.
